# Overview {.unnumbered}

This report prepares the raw SPSS data from **Case 31: Employees Federal Credit Union** for analysis in R. Following the M08 data preparation procedure, I:

1.  give each respondent an ID,
2.  check and fix variable names, variable labels, and value labels,
3.  assign the correct **scale of measurement** to each variable,
4.  handle missing and "no answer / no opinion" codes,
5.  reverse code questions where a higher number meant a *lower* amount of the concept,
6.  run frequencies to check for errors and outliers,
7.  run **reliability** and **factor analysis** on each multi-item measure, and
8.  create a **composite index** for each construct.

::: callout-note
## Data and questionnaire

The raw data file is `data/Case 31 Data_efcu_1.sav` (SPSS format). Questions 1, 2, 28, 29, 35, 36, 39, and 40 are not in the file. Questions 1 and 2 were left out by the credit union because they are sensitive, and the others are open-ended. Every decision below was checked against the questionnaire (Case Exhibit 31.1) and the coding guide (Case Exhibit 31.2).
:::

# Load Packages

```{r}
#| label: packages

# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven", "labelled", "psych"))  # run once if needed
library(tidyverse)  # data wrangling (dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2)
library(haven)      # read SPSS .sav files
library(labelled)   # work with variable and value labels
library(psych)      # reliability (alpha) and factor analysis
```

# Import the Raw Data

```{r}
#| label: import

raw <- read_sav("data/Case 31 Data_efcu_1.sav")
dim(raw)
```

The raw file has **128 respondents** and **34 variables**.

## Data Dictionary (Before Cleaning)

`look_for()` from the **labelled** package builds a data dictionary showing each variable's name, label, and value labels.

```{r}
#| label: dict-before

look_for(raw) |>
  convert_list_columns_to_character() |>
  select(pos, variable, label, value_labels)
```

::: callout-warning
## Problems found in the raw data

- **No respondent ID**, so individual cases cannot be referenced.
- **`q8` has the wrong variable label.** It reads "statement frequency" (a copy of `q9`), but Question 8 asks about the **rates charged to borrow funds**.
- **Incomplete value labels.** Q3 to Q6 and Q30 to Q34 only label 1 and 5; Q13 to Q26 are missing the label for 3 ("Unaware of Service"); Q12 has a value of 3 ("no answer") with no label.
- **`q12` uses 3 for "no answer"** (22 respondents), which must be treated as missing, not as a real answer.
- **Two duplicate composite columns** (`OverallEmployeePerformace` and `employeeperformance`) are identical and unlabeled. I drop them and rebuild the composite myself so the process is documented.
- **Reverse-coded items:** in Q7, Q8, Q9, Q10, Q13 to Q26, and Q37, a *lower* number means *more* of the concept (for example, 1 = "Very High").
:::

```{r}
#| label: duplicate-check

# Confirm the two prebuilt composite columns are identical
all.equal(as.numeric(raw$OverallEmployeePerformace), as.numeric(raw$employeeperformance))
```

# Basic Cleaning

## Respondent ID and Duplicate Columns

```{r}
#| label: id

efcu <- raw |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1) |>
  select(-OverallEmployeePerformace, -employeeperformance)
```

## Variable Labels

I rewrite every variable label to match the wording on the questionnaire. This also fixes the wrong label on `q8`.

```{r}
#| label: var-labels

efcu <- efcu |>
  set_variable_labels(
    id  = "Respondent ID",
    q3  = "Q3. CU employees are courteous",
    q4  = "Q4. CU employees are helpful",
    q5  = "Q5. CU employees are professional",
    q6  = "Q6. CU employees are always available",
    q7  = "Q7. Rates CU pays on share (savings) accounts",
    q8  = "Q8. Rates CU charges members to borrow funds",
    q9  = "Q9. How often you receive a financial statement",
    q10 = "Q10. Accuracy of statements",
    q11 = "Q11. Statements are easy to understand",
    q12 = "Q12. CU keeps account information confidential",
    q13 = "Q13. Awareness: regular share accounts",
    q14 = "Q14. Awareness: special subaccounts",
    q15 = "Q15. Awareness: Christmas club accounts",
    q16 = "Q16. Awareness: individual retirement accounts",
    q17 = "Q17. Awareness: MasterCard credit cards",
    q18 = "Q18. Awareness: signature loans",
    q19 = "Q19. Awareness: new car loans",
    q20 = "Q20. Awareness: late model car loans",
    q21 = "Q21. Awareness: older model car loans",
    q22 = "Q22. Awareness: household goods/appliance loans",
    q23 = "Q23. Awareness: recreational loans",
    q24 = "Q24. Awareness: share collateralized loans",
    q25 = "Q25. Awareness: IRA loans",
    q26 = "Q26. Awareness: line of credit loans",
    q27 = "Q27. Currently have a loan with the CU",
    q30 = "Q30. CU loan rates are lower than other institutions",
    q31 = "Q31. CU personnel keep my financial information confidential",
    q32 = "Q32. CU is prompt in processing loan applications",
    q33 = "Q33. CU services meet the needs of its members",
    q34 = "Q34. CU loan applications are simple and easy",
    q37 = "Q37. Overall, how well the CU is managed and operated",
    q38 = "Q38. Live in the headquarters area"
  )
```

## Value Labels

The labels follow the coding guide in Case Exhibit 31.2. I complete the missing labels so every value has a meaning.

```{r}
#| label: value-labels

agree_5 <- c("Strongly disagree" = 1, "Disagree" = 2, "Uncertain" = 3,
             "Agree" = 4, "Strongly agree" = 5)
yes_no  <- c("Yes" = 1, "No" = 2)
aware_3 <- c("Aware and have used" = 1, "Aware but have not used" = 2,
             "Unaware of service" = 3)

# Helper: apply a set of value labels while keeping each variable label
add_labels <- function(x, labels) {
  labelled(as.numeric(x), labels = labels, label = var_label(x))
}

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(
    across(c(q3:q6, q30:q34), ~ add_labels(.x, agree_5)),
    across(q7:q8, ~ add_labels(.x, c("Very high" = 1, "High" = 2, "Average" = 3,
                                     "Low" = 4, "Very low" = 5, "No opinion" = 6))),
    q9  = add_labels(q9, c("Too often" = 1, "Very often" = 2, "About right" = 3,
                           "Not often enough" = 4, "Never" = 5)),
    q10 = add_labels(q10, c("Excellent" = 1, "Good" = 2, "Fair" = 3, "Poor" = 4)),
    across(c(q11, q27, q38), ~ add_labels(.x, yes_no)),
    q12 = add_labels(q12, c(yes_no, "No answer" = 3)),
    across(q13:q26, ~ add_labels(.x, aware_3)),
    q37 = add_labels(q37, c("Excellent" = 1, "Good" = 2, "Average" = 3,
                            "Poor" = 4, "Very poor" = 5, "No opinion" = 6))
  )
```

## Missing Values and Special Codes

"No opinion" (6) on Q7, Q8, and Q37 and "No answer" (3) on Q12 are not points on the scale, so they become `NA`. In this file, "No opinion" on Q7, Q8, and Q37 was already left blank; the code below makes the rule explicit and catches Q12.

```{r}
#| label: missing

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(
    across(c(q7, q8, q37), ~ replace(.x, .x == 6, NA)),
    q12 = replace(q12, q12 == 3, NA)
  )

# Missing values per variable (only variables with any missing shown)
efcu |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)
```

# Scales of Measurement

Every variable gets a scale of measurement based on what its numbers mean. In R, the scale is expressed through the variable type: **nominal** variables become unordered factors, **ordinal** variables become ordered factors, and **interval** variables stay numeric so they can be averaged.

| Variables | Response format | Scale | R type |
|-----------------|----------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| `id` | Respondent number | Nominal | integer (identifier only) |
| Q3 to Q6, Q30 to Q34 | 5-point Likert, strongly disagree to strongly agree | Interval | numeric |
| Q7, Q8 | Very high to very low | Interval (rating scale, after reverse coding) | numeric |
| Q9 | Too often to never | Ordinal | numeric for recoding, ordered factor for reporting |
| Q10 | Excellent to poor | Interval (rating scale, after reverse coding) | numeric |
| Q37 | Excellent to very poor | Interval (rating scale, after reverse coding) | numeric |
| Q13 to Q26 | Aware and used / aware not used / unaware | Ordinal | numeric for the awareness index |
| Q11, Q12, Q27, Q38 | Yes / No | Nominal | factor |

: Scale of measurement for each variable

::: callout-tip
## Why Likert items are treated as interval

A Likert item has the properties of an ordinal scale (5 is more agreement than 4), and researchers assume the distance between each point is equal. That equal-interval assumption is what lets us **average** items into a composite index.
:::

# Reverse Coding

A higher number should always mean **more** of the concept. In these items the coding guide runs the other way, so I create a new reversed variable with an `r` suffix and keep the original. The formula is **(highest code + 1) minus the original value**.

| Item(s) | Original coding | Formula | New coding |
|-----------------|--------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Q7, Q8 | 1 = very high, 5 = very low | `6 - x` (after "no opinion" set to `NA`) | 1 = very low, 5 = very high |
| Q9 | 1 = too often, 5 = never | `6 - x` | 1 = never, 5 = too often |
| Q10 | 1 = excellent, 4 = poor | `5 - x` | 1 = poor, 4 = excellent |
| Q13 to Q26 | 1 = aware and used, 3 = unaware | `4 - x` | 1 = unaware, 3 = aware and used |
| Q37 | 1 = excellent, 5 = very poor | `6 - x` (after "no opinion" set to `NA`) | 1 = very poor, 5 = excellent |

: Reverse coding plan

```{r}
#| label: reverse

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(
    across(c(q7, q8, q9, q37), ~ 6 - as.numeric(.x), .names = "{.col}r"),
    q10r = 5 - as.numeric(q10),
    across(q13:q26, ~ 4 - as.numeric(.x), .names = "{.col}r")
  )
```

The new variables get their own labels so the direction is clear.

```{r}
#| label: reverse-labels

aware_r <- c("Unaware of service" = 1, "Aware but have not used" = 2,
             "Aware and have used" = 3)

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(
    across(q7r:q8r, ~ add_labels(.x, c("Very low" = 1, "Low" = 2, "Average" = 3,
                                       "High" = 4, "Very high" = 5))),
    q9r  = add_labels(q9r, c("Never" = 1, "Not often enough" = 2, "About right" = 3,
                             "Very often" = 4, "Too often" = 5)),
    q37r = add_labels(q37r, c("Very poor" = 1, "Poor" = 2, "Average" = 3,
                              "Good" = 4, "Excellent" = 5)),
    q10r = add_labels(q10r, c("Poor" = 1, "Fair" = 2, "Good" = 3, "Excellent" = 4)),
    across(q13r:q26r, ~ add_labels(.x, aware_r))
  )

# Copy each original label and add "(reversed)"
for (v in c("q7", "q8", "q9", "q10", paste0("q", 13:26), "q37")) {
  var_label(efcu[[paste0(v, "r")]]) <- paste(var_label(efcu[[v]]), "(reversed)")
}
```

## Check the Recodes

A cross-tab of the original and reversed values confirms each value flipped correctly.

```{r}
#| label: recode-check

efcu |> count(q7, q7r)
efcu |> count(q10, q10r)
efcu |> count(q13, q13r)
efcu |> count(q37, q37r)
```

# Frequencies and Error Checks

## Out-of-Range Values

Every value should fall inside the range allowed by the questionnaire. Any count above zero would signal a data entry error.

```{r}
#| label: range-check

ranges <- tribble(
  ~vars,                                   ~min, ~max,
  c(paste0("q", 3:6), paste0("q", 30:34)), 1,    5,
  c("q7", "q8", "q9", "q37"),              1,    5,
  "q10",                                   1,    4,
  paste0("q", 13:26),                      1,    3,
  c("q11", "q12", "q27", "q38"),           1,    2
)

ranges |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    n_out_of_range = sum(sapply(vars, \(v) {
      x <- as.numeric(efcu[[v]])
      sum(x < min | x > max, na.rm = TRUE)
    })),
    vars = paste(vars, collapse = ", ")
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

All values are within range, so there are no impossible values or outliers to fix.

## Straight-Lining Check

The procedure asks whether anyone answered "all 5's." I check for respondents who gave the identical answer to every agreement item (Q3 to Q6 and Q30 to Q34).

```{r}
#| label: straightline

efcu |>
  mutate(n_unique = apply(across(c(q3:q6, q30:q34), as.numeric), 1,
                          \(r) length(unique(r)))) |>
  filter(n_unique == 1) |>
  select(id, q3:q6, q30:q34)
```

Eight respondents (IDs 1, 5, 6, 10, 62, 70, 77, and 79) gave the same answer to all nine agreement items. None of them answered all 5's; each chose "Agree" (4) or "Uncertain" (3) throughout. A consistent mid-scale pattern is believable for a satisfied but not enthusiastic member, so I **flag but keep** these cases rather than deleting them.

## Frequency Tables

```{r}
#| label: freq-fn

# Frequency table with value labels and valid percentages
freq <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    mutate({{ var }} := as_factor({{ var }})) |>
    count({{ var }}) |>
    mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
}
```

::: panel-tabset
### Employees (Q3 to Q6)

```{r}
#| label: freq-employees

efcu |>
  select(q3:q6) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "item", values_to = "value") |>
  count(item, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = value, values_from = n, values_fill = 0,
              names_sort = TRUE)
```

Most members agree or strongly agree that employees are courteous, helpful, professional, and available. Nobody strongly disagreed with any of the four.

### Rates (Q7r, Q8r)

```{r}
#| label: freq-rates

freq(efcu, q7r)
freq(efcu, q8r)
```

### Statements (Q9 to Q12)

```{r}
#| label: freq-statements

freq(efcu, q9)
freq(efcu, q10r)
freq(efcu, q11)
freq(efcu, q12)
```

### Overall (Q37r, Q38)

```{r}
#| label: freq-overall

freq(efcu, q37r)
freq(efcu, q38)
```
:::

# Multi-Item Measures

The questionnaire has three groups of items that measure one construct together:

| Construct | Items | Name of composite |
|-------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Attitude toward CU employees | Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6 | `att_employee` |
| Attitude toward CU operations and lending | Q30, Q31, Q32, Q33, Q34 | `att_cu` |
| Awareness of CU services | Q13r to Q26r | `awareness` |

: Multi-item measures

For each one, I run a **reliability analysis** (Cronbach's alpha) and an **exploratory factor analysis** before averaging the items. An alpha of **0.70 or higher** is the usual standard for acceptable reliability, and a one-factor solution with loadings of about **0.40 or higher** supports treating the items as one construct.

## Attitude Toward Employees (Q3 to Q6)

```{r}
#| label: rel-employee

emp_items <- efcu |> select(q3:q6) |> mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))
alpha_emp <- psych::alpha(emp_items)
alpha_emp$total |> select(raw_alpha, std.alpha, average_r) |> round(3)
alpha_emp$alpha.drop |> select(raw_alpha) |> round(3)
```

```{r}
#| label: efa-employee

fa_emp <- fa(emp_items, nfactors = 1, fm = "pa")
print(fa_emp$loadings, cutoff = 0)
```

## Attitude Toward CU Operations (Q30 to Q34)

```{r}
#| label: rel-cu

cu_items <- efcu |> select(q30:q34) |> mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))
alpha_cu <- psych::alpha(cu_items)
alpha_cu$total |> select(raw_alpha, std.alpha, average_r) |> round(3)
alpha_cu$alpha.drop |> select(raw_alpha) |> round(3)
```

```{r}
#| label: efa-cu

fa_cu <- fa(cu_items, nfactors = 1, fm = "pa")
print(fa_cu$loadings, cutoff = 0)
```

## Awareness of Services (Q13r to Q26r)

```{r}
#| label: rel-aware

aware_items <- efcu |> select(q13r:q26r) |> mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))
alpha_aware <- psych::alpha(aware_items, check.keys = FALSE)
alpha_aware$total |> select(raw_alpha, std.alpha, average_r) |> round(3)
alpha_aware$alpha.drop |> select(raw_alpha) |> round(3)
```

```{r}
#| label: efa-aware

fa_aware <- fa(aware_items, nfactors = 1, fm = "pa")
print(fa_aware$loadings, cutoff = 0)
```

## Reliability Summary

```{r}
#| label: rel-summary

tibble(
  construct = c("att_employee", "att_cu", "awareness"),
  items     = c("Q3 to Q6", "Q30 to Q34", "Q13r to Q26r"),
  n_items   = c(4, 5, 14),
  alpha     = c(alpha_emp$total$raw_alpha, alpha_cu$total$raw_alpha,
                alpha_aware$total$raw_alpha)
) |>
  mutate(alpha = round(alpha, 3),
         acceptable = if_else(alpha >= 0.70, "Yes", "Below 0.70"))
```

**Interpretation.** Attitude toward employees (alpha = `r sprintf("%.2f", alpha_emp$total$raw_alpha)`) and awareness of services (alpha = `r sprintf("%.2f", alpha_aware$total$raw_alpha)`) both pass the 0.70 standard, and their items load together on a single factor (most loadings near or above 0.40), so they can be combined into composite indexes. No awareness item would raise alpha if dropped.

Attitude toward CU operations (alpha = `r sprintf("%.2f", alpha_cu$total$raw_alpha)`) does **not** meet the standard. Dropping any single item does not fix it, and only Q32 (prompt loan processing) loads strongly on the factor. That makes sense from the questionnaire: Q30 to Q34 ask about different things (loan rates, confidentiality, speed, meeting needs, and simple applications), so they do not measure one underlying attitude. I still build `att_cu` to show the process, but it should be used with caution, and in later analysis these five items are better analyzed **one at a time**.

# Composite Indexes

Each composite is the **row mean** of its items. `rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE)` keeps a respondent who skipped one item instead of dropping them.

```{r}
#| label: composites

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(
    att_employee = rowMeans(across(q3:q6,     as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE),
    att_cu       = rowMeans(across(q30:q34,   as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE),
    awareness    = rowMeans(across(q13r:q26r, as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    att_employee = "Attitude toward CU employees (mean of Q3 to Q6; 1 to 5)",
    att_cu       = "Attitude toward CU operations (mean of Q30 to Q34; 1 to 5)",
    awareness    = "Awareness of CU services (mean of Q13r to Q26r; 1 to 3)"
  )

efcu |>
  select(att_employee, att_cu, awareness) |>
  describe() |>
  select(n, mean, sd, min, max) |>
  round(2)
```

```{r}
#| label: composite-check

# My att_employee matches the composite that came with the raw file
all.equal(as.numeric(efcu$att_employee), as.numeric(raw$employeeperformance))
```

The rebuilt `att_employee` index matches the unlabeled composite that came with the raw file exactly, which confirms that column was the mean of Q3 to Q6.

```{r}
#| label: fig-composites
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the three composite indexes"
#| fig-height: 3.4

efcu |>
  select(att_employee, att_cu, awareness) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "index", values_to = "score") |>
  ggplot(aes(score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#8A4B5E", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ index, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Composite score", y = "Respondents") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#6B2737"))
```

# Nominal Variables as Factors

Yes/no questions are nominal, so they become factors with their labels as the categories.

```{r}
#| label: factors

efcu <- efcu |>
  mutate(across(c(q11, q12, q27, q38), as_factor, .names = "{.col}_f"))

efcu |> count(q38_f)
```

# Save the Cleaned Data

```{r}
#| label: save

write_sav(efcu, "data/case31_efcu_clean.sav")   # keeps labels for SPSS users
write_rds(efcu, "data/case31_efcu_clean.rds")   # keeps labels for R

dim(efcu)
```

The cleaned data set has **`r nrow(efcu)` respondents** and **`r ncol(efcu)` variables**: the original items, an ID, the reversed `r`-suffix items, three composite indexes, and factor versions of the yes/no questions.

## Data Dictionary (After Cleaning)

```{r}
#| label: dict-after

look_for(efcu) |>
  convert_list_columns_to_character() |>
  select(pos, variable, label, value_labels)
```

# Reflection {.unnumbered}

Preparing this data showed me why the M08 procedure matters before any analysis. The raw file looked ready, but it had a wrong variable label on Q8, a "no answer" code hiding inside Q12 that would have been averaged as a real answer, and several items coded so that 1 meant "very high." Reverse coding those items and checking each recode with a cross-tab means that later results read the intuitive way: higher numbers mean more. Running reliability and factor analysis before building the composites also gave me evidence that each set of items measures one idea, instead of just assuming it.
